nodes.label: SMP - what it would take
nodes.rationale: Nothing here is written yet. Counted against the code as it stands rather than estimated, because the last thing written down about SMP was wrong for two years.

nodes.label: The two-year-old SMP claim, corrected
nodes.rationale: CLAUDE.md claimed a per-CPU struct, TPIDR_EL1 and a per-CPU runqueue from the repository's first commit, and none of the three has ever existed. It was an intention written in the present tense that nothing ever went back to.

nodes.label: Not a lock or an atomic anywhere in the kernel
nodes.rationale: Mutual exclusion today is one sentence - there is one core, and the kernel runs with interrupts masked - and every data structure rests on it. That is the correct design for a uniprocessor and it is why ipc.c is 801 lines instead of two thousand. It does mean SMP changes the assumption the whole kernel rests on.

nodes.label: The six things that have to become per-CPU
nodes.rationale: current, idle_thread, idle_ticks/busy_ticks, the FP owner, the runqueue (head[], tail[], occupied), and the TSS / kernel stack. This is the whole of what 'a per-CPU struct' means, made concrete.

nodes.label: The register that finds the per-CPU struct
nodes.rationale: TPIDR_EL1 on AArch64, the GS base with swapgs on x86-64. Neither is written. The smallest piece of the work and the one that touches the most files, because every exception entry has to establish it before anything else runs.

nodes.label: The user_rsp bug - per-CPU vs per-thread
nodes.rationale: A global holding the interrupted stack pointer looked like per-CPU state, was per-thread, and one core was enough to prove it wrong: a process that blocked in IPC let another run and the second overwrote the first's. Found the expensive way, which is the only way it gets found.

nodes.label: The pools are the easy locks
nodes.rationale: threads[], processes[], endpoints[], objects[] and the physical bitmap are arrays with an allocation function each. One lock apiece around allocate and free is correct and uncontended.

nodes.label: Capabilities are already nearly safe
nodes.rationale: They live in struct thread as caps[CAPS_PER_THREAD], so a thread's table is touched by that thread and nobody else - except when one is granted, which is the one path that needs care. Luck worth naming.

nodes.label: IPC is the hard one
nodes.rationale: send, receive and reply each touch two threads and an endpoint at once, and the states they move through have to change together or a message is delivered twice, or to a thread that has since died. 801 lines, every one assuming nothing else is running.

nodes.label: deliver wakes the peer and enqueues rather than switching to it
nodes.rationale: A direct handoff would be faster and would mean one core writing another core's stack. The slower shape is the one that survives SMP.

nodes.label: PSCI CPU_ON - ARM bring-up is nearly free
nodes.rationale: hal/qemu-virt/power.c already uses PSCI to turn the machine off, and CPU_ON is the same call with a different function id and an entry point. The GIC already gives software-generated interrupts, which is what an IPI is.

nodes.label: x86-64 SMP is a new driver: local APIC and ACPI MADT
nodes.rationale: Kosmos drives the 8259 PIC. SMP needs the local APIC for IPIs and a per-core timer, because one 8253 cannot tick four cores, plus ACPI MADT parsing to find the cores and their APIC ids. That is a table walker and an interrupt controller, neither of which exists - most of the reason the two boards are not equal work. Then INIT-SIPI-SIPI and a real-mode trampoline page under 1 MB.

nodes.label: Do SMP on AArch64 first
nodes.source_location: The order, and why ARM first
nodes.rationale: x86-64 is total-store-ordered and forgives reorderings AArch64 does not. A locking discipline correct on ARM is correct on x86; one developed on x86 will be wrong on ARM in ways that appear once every few thousand boots, the most expensive class of bug this project has.

nodes.label: The seven-step order
nodes.source_location: The order, and why ARM first
nodes.rationale: Per-CPU struct with NR_CPUS = 1; locks taken uncontended on one core; a second core parked; the idle thread on it; per-CPU runqueues; IPIs; TLB shootdown. The kernel is correct at every step and make test still passes, which is what makes it safe incrementally.

nodes.label: Per-CPU runqueues behind the scheduler vtable
nodes.source_location: The order, and why ARM first
nodes.rationale: struct scheduler in sched.h is already a vtable, so this is a policy beside sched_prio.c rather than surgery on it - the one place the existing design genuinely is ready.

nodes.label: IPIs for preempting a remote core
nodes.source_location: The order, and why ARM first
nodes.rationale: Without this a high-priority thread waits for the other core's quantum, and the whole responsiveness argument dies.

nodes.label: TLB shootdown as the last step
nodes.source_location: The order, and why ARM first
nodes.rationale: as_switch invalidates locally with tlbi vmalle1; with two cores in one address space, unmapping needs the other core told.

nodes.label: What SMP would cost, honestly
nodes.rationale: The x86-64 port was the same design against different registers. SMP is not that: it changes the invariant every file in kernel/ was written against, and the work is spread thin across all of them rather than concentrated in a new directory. Bring-up is a week of fiddly well-documented work; the locking is where the time goes and IPC is where the bugs will be.

nodes.label: make stress becomes the SMP test
nodes.rationale: It already asks the right question - use the machine hard, then ask sysinfo whether it gave everything back - because a lost lock shows up as a leaked slot. What it cannot do is find an ordering bug, and nothing can reliably.

nodes.label: Not in scope: load balancing, affinity, lock-free
nodes.rationale: Those are optimisations of a thing that has to exist and be correct first, and this project has been bitten before by optimising ahead of a measurement.
